# Sirach Chapter 9 — Disagreement Log

**Date:** 2026-03-17
**Chapter:** Sirach 9 (18 verses)
**Agents:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Total Disagreements:** 14

---

## Disagreement 001 — v.1: "teach her a wicked lesson against yourself" vs. "teach her a harmful lesson at your own expense"

**EMET:** "lest you teach her a wicked lesson against yourself"
**LOGOS:** "you will teach her a harmful lesson at your own expense"
**PNEUMA:** "you'll end up teaching your wife tricks she can use against you"
**Issue:** Greek mē paideusēs ep' autō kakian = "do not teach evil against yourself." The idea is: jealousy backfires by teaching the wife how to deceive. EMET "wicked lesson" is literal. LOGOS "harmful lesson at your own expense" is clearer. Consensus: LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 002 — v.2: "give a woman power over your soul" vs. "surrender yourself to a woman"

**EMET:** "Do not give a woman power over your soul"
**LOGOS:** "Do not surrender yourself to a woman so that she gains control over you"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't surrender your heart to a woman to the point where she controls you"
**Issue:** Greek mē dōs gynaikī tēn psychēn sou = "do not give a woman your soul." EMET is most literal. Consensus: "Do not give a woman power over your soul."

---

## Disagreement 003 — v.3: "strange woman" vs. "loose woman"

**EMET:** "Do not go to meet a strange woman"
**LOGOS:** "Do not go near a loose woman"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't go near a promiscuous woman"
**Issue:** Greek allotriai = "alien/foreign woman" — a euphemism in wisdom literature (cf. Proverbs) for a sexually dangerous woman. EMET's "strange" is literal but potentially obscure. LOGOS "loose" is more idiomatic. Consensus: "Do not approach a loose woman."

---

## Disagreement 004 — v.4: "singing woman" vs. "female entertainer"

**EMET:** "Do not associate with a singing woman"
**LOGOS:** "Do not keep company with a female entertainer"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't spend time with female performers"
**Issue:** Greek psallousē = "one who plays/sings." EMET's "singing woman" is literal. In context, the reference is to professional female entertainers at banquets, often associated with loose morals. Consensus: "a singing woman" preserved as most literal.

---

## Disagreement 005 — v.5: "stumble and incur penalties" vs. "stumble and pay a penalty"

**EMET:** "lest you stumble and incur penalties for her"
**LOGOS:** "lest you be ensnared and pay a penalty for it"
**PNEUMA:** "you'll stumble into trouble and face consequences"
**Issue:** Greek mē porneuthēs ep' autē = "lest you be ensnared/destroyed over her." The penalty was legal — intercourse with an unmarried virgin had legal consequences. LOGOS "pay a penalty" is clearest. Consensus: LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 006 — v.6: "give your soul to harlots" vs. "give yourself to prostitutes"

**EMET:** "Do not give your soul to harlots"
**LOGOS:** "Do not give yourself to prostitutes"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't waste yourself on prostitutes"
**Issue:** Greek pornais mē ekdous tēn psychēn sou = "do not give your soul to prostitutes." EMET's "harlots" is archaic; "prostitutes" is clearer. Consensus: "Do not give yourself to prostitutes."

---

## Disagreement 007 — v.7: "roam the deserted parts" vs. "wander its lonely places"

**EMET:** "nor roam the deserted parts of it"
**LOGOS:** "nor wander its lonely places"
**PNEUMA:** "Don't hang around in desolate parts of the city"
**Issue:** Greek eremia = "wilderness/desolate." The warning is about places where one might encounter loose women or criminals. Consensus: LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 008 — v.8: "shapely woman" vs. "beautiful woman"

**EMET:** "Turn away your eye from a shapely woman"
**LOGOS:** "Turn your eyes away from a beautiful woman"
**PNEUMA:** "Look away from a woman who is beautiful"
**Issue:** Greek gynaikos = "woman" with no adjective in all versions — the adjective comes from context. Greek eumorphias = "good form/beauty." EMET's "shapely" is specific to physical form. Consensus: "Turn your eye away from a beautiful woman."

---

## Disagreement 009 — v.9: "recline beside a married woman" vs. "recline next to a married woman at table"

**EMET:** "Never recline beside a married woman"
**LOGOS:** "Never recline next to a married woman at table"
**PNEUMA:** "Never lie down next to a married woman at a banquet"
**Issue:** Greek meta hyandros gynaikos = "with a married woman." The context is the symposium — reclining at dinner. LOGOS makes the setting explicit. Consensus: "Never recline beside a married woman at table."

---

## Disagreement 010 — v.10: "does not compare with him" vs. "cannot match him"

**EMET:** "a new one does not compare with him"
**LOGOS:** "a new one cannot match him"
**PNEUMA:** "No new friend can replace him"
**Issue:** Greek ou sygkrineitai autō = "is not compared to him." LOGOS "cannot match" is elegant. Consensus: LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 011 — v.12: "not go unpunished to their grave" vs. "not remain unpunished until they die"

**EMET:** "they will not go unpunished to their grave"
**LOGOS:** "they will not remain unpunished until they die"
**PNEUMA:** "they will not escape to the grave without punishment"
**Issue:** Greek hoti ou mē atōōthēsin heōs hadou = "for they will not go unpunished as far as Hades." EMET "to their grave" captures Hades. Consensus: EMET.

---

## Disagreement 012 — v.13: "haunted by the fear of death" vs. "no fear of death"

**EMET:** "you will not be haunted by the fear of death"
**LOGOS:** "you will have no fear of death"
**PNEUMA:** "you won't be living in fear of death"
**Issue:** Greek mē phobou = "do not fear death." EMET adds "haunted" — slightly interpretive. Consensus: "you will not fear death."

---

## Disagreement 013 — v.15: "men of understanding" vs. "perceptive people"

**EMET:** "Let your conversation be with men of understanding"
**LOGOS:** "Let your conversation be with perceptive people"
**PNEUMA:** "Let your conversations be with people of real understanding"
**Issue:** Greek syneton = "discerning/understanding." "Men of understanding" (EMET) is more traditional; "perceptive people" (LOGOS) is more neutral. Consensus: "people of understanding."

---

## Disagreement 014 — v.18: "talkative person is dangerous" vs. "person of loose speech is a danger"

**EMET:** "A talkative person is dangerous in his city"
**LOGOS:** "A person of loose speech is a danger in a city"
**PNEUMA:** "A person who talks too freely is a hazard to their community"
**Issue:** Greek polyglōssos = "many-tongued/talkative." The issue is irresponsible talk, not just quantity. "Loose speech" (LOGOS) captures the quality. Consensus: LOGOS.

---
